Finally, this section considers the future trajectory of libraries in an ever-more digital 
world. 
4.1.1 Drivers of Digital Transformation 
Several key factors are pushing libraries to embrace digital transformation. One 
primary driver is the evolving expectations of library patrons, especially younger 
generations who have grown up in a digital-ﬁrst world [ 
11]. Today’s users expect 
information and services to be available online anytime, anywhere, and from any 
device. They want personalized, interactive experiences akin to what they get from 
companies like Amazon and Netﬂix. Traditional library services centered around 
physical collections are no longer sufﬁcient. 
Competition from other information providers is also spurring libraries to trans-
form. In the past, libraries held a near-monopoly on information access. But now 
patrons can turn to Google, Wikipedia, and countless other online sources to get the 
information they need, often more quickly and conveniently than from a library [ 56]. 
To stay relevant, libraries must offer digital resources and services that are as good 
as or better than what patrons can ﬁnd elsewhere [ 14]. 
Another driver of digital transformation is the need to increase efﬁciency and 
reduce costs. Many libraries, especially public libraries, have seen their budgets 
slashed in recent years [ 51]. At the same time, the volume of information is explod-
ing, and patron demands are rising. Digital technologies allow libraries to automate 
processes, share resources, and serve more patrons with less work on the staff. Tools

4.1 Introduction to Digital Transformation in Libraries 103
like self-checkout kiosks, automated storage and retrieval systems, and chatbots are 
helping libraries do more with less. 
The COVID-19 pandemic dramatically accelerated the digital transformation of 
libraries. 
With physical locations closed, libraries had to pivot quickly to providing 
all services online. Patrons who may have never used digital library resources before 
were suddenly reliant on them. Programs like virtual storytimes, online book clubs, 
and remote reference services became commonplace [ 51 ]. The pandemic made clear 
that 
robust digital offerings are essential for libraries to fulﬁll their missions in times 
of crisis and beyond. 
4.1.2 Opportunities and Innovations 
Digital transformation presents many exciting opportunities for libraries to serve their 
communities better. One key area is improving access to collections and resources. 
Digitization projects are making rare and unique materials available to patrons around 
the world [ 119]. Through digital repositories and open access initiatives, libraries 
are 
unlocking scholarly research previously hidden behind paywalls [ 107]. Collab-
orati
ve efforts like HathiTrust and the Digital Public Library of America combine 
content from libraries and other cultural heritage organizations into shared discov-
ery platforms, enabling patrons to ﬁnd a wealth of information through a single 
search [ 28]. 
Libraries also use digital technologies to create new types of content and services. 
Mak
erspaces and digital media labs allow patrons to learn new skills and use cutting-
edge equipment to create podcasts, videos, 3D prints, and more [ 87]. Libraries are 
de
veloping mobile apps to put library services in the palms of patrons’ hands [ 17]. 
Augmented 
and virtual reality are being used for immersive learning experiences, 
from virtual museum tours to STEM simulations [ 13]. Through social media and 
cro
wdsourcing, libraries engage patrons in new ways to co-create knowledge and 
collections. 
AI and big data are opening possibilities for libraries to provide more personalized 
services. 
By analyzing patron interactions and preferences data, libraries can provide 
targeted reading recommendations, research assistance, and learning resources to 
individual users [ 54]. AI-powered chatbots can answer basic reference questions, 
freeing 
up staff for higher-level support [ 6]. Machine Learning (ML) can help libraries 
better 
understand and predict patron needs [137 ]. 
The Internet of Things is also beginning to impact libraries. Smart sensors and data 
analytics 
create responsive library environments that automatically adjust lighting, 
temperature, and noise levels for optimal patron comfort and energy efﬁciency [ 139]. 
Bluetooth 
beacons and RFID tags enable intelligent wayﬁnding and self-guided tours 
within library spaces [ 5]. Intelligent return and sorting systems are speeding up 
collection 
management [ 122]. 
As more library services move online and into the cloud, ensuring equitable access 
is 
paramount. Libraries play a vital role in bridging the digital divide for underserved

104 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
populations by providing access to devices, high-speed internet, and technology train-
ing [112 ]. Librarians also teach data and information literacy skills to help patrons 
na
vigate online information and spot misinformation [ 70]. Through partnerships with 
schools 
and community organizations, libraries are meeting patrons where they are 
to deliver digital services and resources [ 62]. 
4.1.3 Challenges and Future Directions 
While digital transformation holds much promise for libraries, it also presents many 
challenges. One is the constant change and unpredictability of technology. Libraries 
must continually adapt to new devices, platforms, and patron expectations. Keeping 
staff skills up-to-date and maintaining aging systems while investing in innovations 
[ 16] can be difﬁcult. Balancing the needs of tech-savvy and traditional patrons is 
also 
a challenge. 
Funding is another major hurdle. While some libraries have secured grants or 
pri
vate funding for digital initiatives, many struggle to ﬁnd room for the technology, 
staff, and training needed for actual digital transformation [108 ]. Demonstrating the 
v
alue and impact of new digital services can be difﬁcult using traditional library 
metrics. 
Other challenges include copyright and licensing issues around digital content, 
protecting 
patron data privacy, and digital preservation of born-digital and digitized 
materials. Libraries must also grapple with complex ethical issues raised by data 
analytics, surveillance, and automated decision-making systems [ 71]. 
As technologies like AI, virtual/augmented reality, and the Internet of Things 
continue 
to advance, they will undoubtedly reshape libraries even further [ 63]. It is 
dif
ﬁcult to predict exactly what libraries will look like decades from now, but some 
potential future developments include:
. Fully automated and personalized library services informed by patron data.
. All-digital, instantly accessible collections with print materials stored offsite.
. Libraries as community hubs for digital creation, collaboration, and engagement.
. Librarians as data scientists and information technology experts.
. Responsive, sensor-enabled library buildings that adapt to individual patron needs.
. Gamiﬁcation and immersive storytelling woven throughout library programs and 
spaces.
. Seamless integration of library services and content into virtual learning environ-
ments.
. Shared, globally networked library platforms and infrastructure. 
To prepare for this future, libraries must cultivate a culture of innovation, exper-
imentation, 
and continuous learning. Library staff will need ongoing training to 
keep their digital skills sharp. Library leaders must advocate for sustainable funding 
and partnerships to support digital transformation [ 51]. Most importantly, libraries

4.2 From Physical to Digital: The Transition of Library Mediums 105
must keep their communities at the center of digital initiatives, ensuring that new 
technologies and services are accessible, inclusive, and responsive to local needs 
[ 49]. 
In conclusion, digital transformation presents immense challenges and opportuni-
ties 
for libraries. By embracing new technologies and reimagining services, spaces, 
and roles, libraries can remain vital community institutions for generations. The path 
forward is not about chasing the latest technological trends but strategically leverag-
ing digital tools and platforms to advance the enduring mission of libraries to provide 
equitable access to information, support lifelong learning, and strengthen commu-
nities. With a spirit of innovation and collaboration, libraries can adapt to and help 
shape the digital future. 
4.2 From Physical to Digital: The Transition of Library 
Mediums 
Over the past few decades, libraries have transformed from physical spaces hous-
ing print collections to digital hubs providing round-the-clock access to vast elec-
tronic resources. Rapid technological advancements, shifting user expectations, and 
the imperative to preserve fragile physical collections have propelled this transi-
tion from analog to digital. While digitization presents myriad opportunities for 
libraries to expand access and innovate services, it also poses challenges related to 
copyright, cost, technical infrastructure, and staff expertise. This subsection delves 
into the critical aspects of the shift from physical to digital libraries, examining the 
drivers of change, beneﬁts and challenges, technologies and processes involved, and 
implications for the future of libraries and librarianship. 
4.2.1 Drivers of the Digital Transition 
A conﬂuence of factors has accelerated libraries’ adoption of digital technologies and 
resources. Technological advances, particularly the rise of computers, the internet, 
and digital storage, have made it possible to convert analog materials into elec-
tronic formats that can be readily duplicated, transmitted, and accessed from any-
where [ 73]. Mass digitization projects like Google Books have demonstrated the 
feasibility 
of scanning millions of print volumes [ 36]. Concomitantly, improvements 
in 
digital cameras, scanners, and optical character recognition (OCR) have rendered 
digitization faster and more cost-effective. 
User demand has also played a pivotal role in driving the digital transition. Library 
patrons, 
especially digital natives, increasingly expect information to be available

106 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
online and accessible across devices [ 86]. Students and researchers value the con-
v
enience of accessing library resources remotely, a trend that surged during the 
COVID-19 pandemic as physical libraries closed [ 111]. 
Moreover, space constraints have compelled many libraries, particularly academic 
ones, 
to grapple with the challenge of accommodating growing print collections. Dig-
itizing older, lesser-used materials liberates valuable shelf space while maintaining 
content accessibility. Some libraries are relocating print volumes to offsite storage 
and providing digital or scan-on-demand access [ 118]. 
Preservation constitutes another signiﬁcant driver of digitization. Digital surro-
g
ates can safeguard fragile or deteriorating originals from further damage caused 
by physical handling [ 33]. When coupled with a robust digital preservation strategy, 
digitization 
can help ensure long-term access as analog formats degrade or become 
obsolete [ 35]. However, it is crucial to recognize that digitization is not a one-time 
process; 
digital ﬁles also necessitate ongoing maintenance and migration [ 50]. 
4.2.2 Beneﬁts of Going Digital 
Transitioning collections and services to digital platforms offers many potential ben-
eﬁts for libraries and their users. Foremost among these is increased access. Digital 
content can be accessed remotely 24/7, transcending the library’s physical bound-
aries and expanding its reach. Users are no longer constrained by library hours or 
geographic location. Materials previously restricted, such as rare books or special 
collections, can be made widely available online, enabling libraries to share their 
unique content with a global audience [ 33]. 
Enhanced discoverability is another crucial beneﬁt of digitization. Digital ﬁles 
can 
be indexed and made full-text searchable, empowering users to quickly locate 
relevant information within documents [ 72 ]. Descriptive metadata renders digital 
content 
more discoverable in library catalogs, search engines, and digital repositories. 
Linked data can establish connections between related resources across collections 
and institutions. 
Digitization also unlocks new possibilities for content use and analysis. Text 
and 
data mining techniques can uncover novel insights and relationships within and 
across documents [101 ]. Digital humanities projects can combine library collections 
with 
computational analysis and visualization tools to explore innovative research 
questions. APIs can facilitate new services and integrations with library resources. 
Furthermore, digitization can serve as a preservation strategy by creating sur-
rog
ate copies of deteriorating or at-risk analog materials [ 33]. However, effective 
digital 
preservation requires ongoing management, including refreshing storage 
media, migrating ﬁles to new formats, and maintaining multiple copies in distributed 
locations. 
Converting print materials to digital formats can also alleviate pressures on library 
space 
and storage costs [ 81]. Lesser-used materials can be moved to compact shelving

4.2 From Physical to Digital: The Transition of Library Mediums 107
or offsite facilities, with digital copies available. However, many libraries adopt a 
hybrid approach, retaining print originals even after digitization. 
While digitization entails signiﬁcant upfront costs, it may yield savings over time 
compared 
to the expenses associated with physical storage, circulation, and preserva-
tion. Digital resources circumvent reshelving, repairs, binding, and loss costs. More-
over, digital content can be readily duplicated and shared across libraries through 
consortial licensing and interlibrary loan [ 135]. 
4.2.3 Challenges of Digitization 
Despite the numerous beneﬁts, libraries face various challenges in shifting to . Copy-
right stands as a major barrier to digitization. Many books and journals remain under 
copyright protection, restricting libraries’ ability to digitize and provide access with-
out permission from rights holders [ 131]. Obtaining permissions is time-consuming 
and 
costly. Fair use and copyright exceptions for libraries are not always clear-cut in 
the digital environment. Orphan works, whose rights holders cannot be identiﬁed or 
located, pose another challenge. 
Cost represents another signiﬁcant hurdle. Digitization and digital preservation 
are 
expensive undertakings, demanding substantial investments in technology, infras-
tructure, and expertise. While grants and one-time funding may cover initial costs, 
ongoing expenses must be integrated into budgets. Smaller institutions may lack the 
resources to digitize at scale. Partnerships and collaborative projects can help share 
costs and expertise [ 135]. 
Digitization also requires specialized skills and knowledge that library staff may 
not 
possess [ 26]. Staff need training in imaging standards, metadata creation, digital 
preserv
ation, and project management. Libraries may need to establish new digital 
curation positions or outsource to vendors. Sustaining expertise can be challenging 
with grant-funded, term-limited positions. 
Storing, managing, and providing access to sizeable digital collections neces-
sitates 
robust technical infrastructure, including storage systems, repositories, and 
discovery platforms. Existing library systems designed for print materials may not 
be well-suited for managing digital content. Libraries require scalable, interoperable, 
and standards-based infrastructure that can evolve with technological changes [ 130]. 
Making digital content discoverable by users is an ongoing challenge. Libraries 
must 
create high-quality, standards-based metadata to support discovery within and 
across collections. Search tools and interfaces need to be intuitive and accessible. 
Digital content should be integrated with other library discovery systems and open 
to crawling by search engines. Consistent and persistent identiﬁers are essential for 
managing and citing digital content over time [ 101]. 
Ensuring long-term access to digital content is a critical challenge. Digital ﬁles 
are 
vulnerable to loss and obsolescence due to technological change, bit rot, and 
organizational failures. Libraries need sustainable digital preservation strategies that

108 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
encompass distributed and redundant storage, active management, and migration. 
Preservation efforts must be integrated into digitization projects from the outset [ 33]. 
Libraries must also design effective and user-friendly interfaces for accessing 
digital 
collections. Users expect fast, intuitive, and seamless discovery and access 
across devices [ 31]. Libraries must balance ease of access with necessary restrictions 
based 
on copyright, licensing, and privacy concerns. Accessible design for users with 
disabilities is crucial. 
4.2.4 Digitization Technologies and Processes 
Converting physical library materials to digital formats involves a range of technolo-
gies and workﬂows. Digitization typically begins with imaging physical materials 
using digital cameras or scanners. Archival standards call for high-resolution, loss-
less master ﬁles in formats like TIFF. Master ﬁles are large and require signiﬁcant 
storage. Derivative ﬁles in smaller sizes and formats like JPEG are created for access. 
Optical character recognition (OCR) converts page images to machine-readable text 
to enable full-text search [ 53]. 
Analog audiovisual materials like cassette tapes and VHS require specialized 
equipment 
and expertise to digitize. Preservation-quality standards specify uncom-
pressed or lossless formats at high bit depths and sampling rates. Digitization must be 
done in real-time and is thus labor-intensive. Many analog formats risk degradation 
and obsolescence, making digitization an urgent need [ 53]. 
Descriptive, technical, and administrative metadata are essential for managing 
and 
providing access to digital collections. Metadata schemas like Dublin Core 
and MODS provide standard structures. Controlled vocabulary enables consistent 
description. Metadata can be created manually, repurposed from existing records, 
or extracted automatically [ 104]. Metadata is stored in databases, encoded in XML, 
and 
exposed to the web using standards like OAI-PMH and Linked Data [ 145]. 
Digital asset management systems (DAMS) and institutional repositories provide 
platforms 
for organizing, storing, and providing access to digital collections. These 
systems support metadata management, indexing, search, and retrieval. Examples 
include Fedora, DSpace, CONTENTdm, and Islandora. Many are open source but 
require signiﬁcant local implementation and support [ 12]. 
Libraries provide access to digital collections through various channels, including 
library 
websites, discovery layers, digital exhibits, and third-party aggregators. User 
authentication may be required for licensed resources. Streaming servers are used 
for audiovisual content. APIs allow programmatic access and integration. Digital 
collections should be optimized for search engines and social media sharing [ 12]. 
Digital preservation involves actively managing ﬁles over time to ensure long-term 
access. 
Strategies include refreshing storage media, replicating content in multiple 
locations, migrating ﬁles to new formats, and maintaining software and hardware 
dependencies. The Open Archival Information System (OAIS) provides a conceptual 
framework [ 32]. Speciﬁc tools include Archivematica, BitCurator, and Preservica.

4.2 From Physical to Digital: The Transition of Library Mediums 109
4.2.5 Future Directions 
As technology evolves, libraries must adapt their approaches to collections, services, 
and spaces. Libraries are shifting from siloed catalogs to interoperable linked data 
that connects information across the web. Linked data standards like BIBFRAME and 
schema.org enable library metadata to be integrated with other web resources [
103]. 
This will make library collections more discoverable and reusable, enabling new 
services and research uses. 
AI and ML tools can automate and enhance various aspects of digital collec-
tions, from metadata creation to content analysis [ 102]. ML can extract features 
from images, transcribe handwritten text, identify entities in documents, and clas-
sify materials. These tools can supplement human labor and enable new modes of 
discovery and analysis. 
Libraries increasingly support digital scholarship activities, such as text mining, 
data visualization, and digital publishing. This may involve providing access to digital 
collections, tools, and expertise. Libraries are creating spaces and services to facilitate 
digital research and pedagogy, such as makerspaces and digital humanities centers. 
Libraries also advocate for open access to research outputs and cultural heritage 
materials. This includes digitizing and making freely available public domain works, 
negotiating open access rights with publishers, and supporting faculty in depositing 
works in institutional repositories [ 126]. Open access expands the reach and impact 
of library collections and democratizes access to knowledge. 
Furthermore, libraries play a crucial role in bridging the digital divide and ensuring 
equitable access to information and technology [ 66]. This includes providing access 
to computers and the internet, digital literacy training, and assistive technologies. As 
more library resources and services move online, it is critical to consider the needs 
of marginalized communities and design for accessibility and inclusion. 
4.2.6 Libraries’ Digital Evolution 
The transition from physical to digital collections and services is transforming the 
role and identity of libraries in the 21st century. Digitization offers vast opportunities 
to expand access to information, preserve cultural heritage, and enable new forms of 
research and engagement [
102]. However, it presents complex copyright, funding, 
technology, and organizational change challenges. Libraries must balance the needs 
and expectations of diverse users, prioritize investments with limited resources, and 
continuously adapt to new technologies and standards. 
Despite the challenges, the future of libraries is undeniably digital. Patrons 
increasingly expect information to be available online and accessible anytime, any-
where [ 
66]. The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the shift to digital services 
and highlighted the critical importance of robust digital infrastructure and expertise.

110 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
At the same time, physical libraries remain vital community hubs and cultural insti-
tutions. The role of librarians is evolving to encompass new skills in digital curation, 
data management, and online instruction [ 80]. 
As libraries navigate this digital transition, it is essential to center core values 
of access, equity, privacy, and preservation. Libraries must advocate for the public 
interest in the digital age and work to ensure that knowledge and culture are accessible 
to all. This will require collaboration across institutions, sectors, and communities 
to build shared infrastructure, standards, and practices. It will also require sustained 
investment and support from funding bodies and stakeholders. 
Ultimately, the transition from physical to digital is not a simple one-to-one trans-
fer but a complex transformation that fundamentally reshapes the nature and scope of 
libraries. It requires reimagining the library as a platform for discovery, creation, and 
collaboration that transcends the limitations of physical space and collections. By 
embracing the opportunities and challenges of the digital age, libraries can continue 
to fulﬁll their vital mission of empowering individuals and communities through 
knowledge and information. 
4.3 Integration of Digital Formats in Library Collections 
In the digital age, libraries face the challenge of integrating digital formats into their 
collections alongside traditional print materials. This integration directly results from 
the rapid advancement of digital technologies, which have transformed how libraries 
collect, organize, preserve, and provide access to information resources. As modern 
libraries adapt to meet their users’ evolving needs and expectations, they must nav-
igate the opportunities and challenges presented by this digital transformation [ 
76]. 
The following subsections will explore the importance of integrating digital formats; 
the challenges libraries face, best practices for successful integration, and the con-
cept of “phygital” experiences that blend physical and digital elements. Finally, we 
will consider the future of digital integration in libraries and the ongoing need for 
innovation, sustainability, and accessibility in the face of an ever-changing digital 
landscape. 
4.3.1 The Importance of Integrating Digital Formats 
Integrating digital formats into library collections is crucial for several reasons. First, 
it allows libraries to provide access to a broader range of information resources, 
including born-digital content and digitized versions of print materials (Trivedi, 
2010) [
130]. This expanded access is particularly important in an era where users 
expect to be able to access information anytime, anywhere, and from any device 
(Library of Congress, 2021) [ 
76].

4.3 Integration of Digital Formats in Library Collections 111
Second, digital formats offer new possibilities for organizing, discovering, and 
interacting with information. For example, digital collections can be searched and 
browsed in ways that are not possible with physical collections, such as full-text 
searching and faceted navigation [
130]. Digital formats also enable libraries to cre-
ate interactive and immersive user experiences, such as virtual exhibits and digital 
storytelling. 
Third, integrating digital formats can help libraries preserve and protect their col-
lections. Digital preservation strategies, such as creating multiple copies and migrat-
ing content to new formats, can help ensure the long-term accessibility of digital 
resources [ 
76]. Additionally, digitizing fragile or rare materials can help protect the 
original items from damage while providing access to the content [ 130]. 
4.3.2 Challenges of Integrating Digital Formats 
Despite the many beneﬁts of integrating digital formats, libraries face several chal-
lenges. One major challenge is the rapid pace of technological change, making it 
difﬁcult for libraries to keep up with new formats and standards [ 
4]. As new tech-
nologies emerge, libraries must continually adapt their systems and workﬂows to 
ensure digital content remains accessible and usable over time. 
Another challenge is the complexity of managing hybrid collections that include 
both print and digital materials. Integrating these different formats requires care-
ful planning and coordination to ensure they are correctly cataloged, preserved, 
and made discoverable to users. This can be particularly challenging when dealing 
with large-scale digital collections or when integrating digital content from multiple 
sources [ 
76]. 
A third challenge is developing new skills and expertise among library staff. 
Managing digital collections requires a range of technical skills, such as digital 
preservation, metadata creation, and web development [
27, 65]. Libraries must invest 
in training and professional development to ensure staff have the knowledge and skills 
to manage digital content effectively. 
4.3.3 Best Practices for Integrating Digital Formats 
To successfully integrate digital formats into their collections, libraries should follow 
several best practices. First, libraries should develop clear policies and procedures 
for acquiring, organizing, preserving, and providing access to digital content [ 76]. 
These policies should be based on a thorough understanding of user needs and align 
with the library’s mission and goals. 
Second, libraries should use standards-based approaches for creating and man-
aging digital content. This includes using established metadata standards, such as

112 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
Dublin Core and MODS, to ensure digital content is consistently described, eas-
ily shared, and integrated with other systems. Libraries should also use open for-
mats and protocols wherever possible to maximize interoperability and long-term 
accessibility [145 ]. 
Third, libraries should prioritize user experience when designing digital col-
lections 
and services. This means creating intuitive interfaces allowing users to 
discover, access, and interact with digital content quickly. It also means provid-
ing clear guidance and support to help users navigate the complexities of digital 
collections [ 130]. 
Fourth, libraries should collaborate with other institutions and organizations to 
share 
resources and expertise related to digital collections. This can include par-
ticipating in consortia or networks that facilitate sharing digital content and best 
practices [ 76]. It can also involve partnering with faculty, researchers, and other 
stak
eholders to develop digital collections that support speciﬁc research or teaching 
needs. 
Finally, libraries should continuously assess and evaluate their digital collections 
and 
services to ensure that they meet user needs and achieve desired outcomes. 
This can involve collecting usage data, conducting user surveys or focus groups, 
and regularly reviewing and updating policies and procedures [ 76]. By taking an 
e
vidence-based approach to managing digital collections, libraries can ensure that 
they are making the most effective use of their resources and providing the most 
outstanding value to their users. 
4.3.4 Phygital Experiences: Blending Physical and Digital 
As libraries integrate digital formats into their collections, they are also exploring 
new ways to blend physical and digital experiences for their users. This trend, known 
as “phygital” experiences, seeks to create seamless and immersive user experiences 
that combine the best of both worlds [ 94, 100]. 
One example of a phygital experience in libraries is using augmented reality 
(AR) 
to enhance physical collections. Users can scan physical objects or spaces 
in the library using AR apps or devices and access related digital content, such as 
videos, 3D models, or historical information [ 100]. This allows users to engage with 
library 
collections in new and interactive ways while maintaining a connection to the 
physical space. 
Another example is using digital kiosks or interactive displays in library spaces. 
These 
displays can provide access to digital collections, allow users to explore virtual 
exhibits, or enable them to create and share their digital content [ 94]. By integrating 
digital 
experiences into physical spaces, libraries can create more engaging and 
participatory environments for their users. 
Phygital experiences can also extend beyond the library walls. For example, 
libraries 
can create mobile apps that allow users to access digital collections and 
services from anywhere while maintaining a connection to the physical library [ 55 ].

4.3 Integration of Digital Formats in Library Collections 113
They can also partner with other cultural institutions, such as museums or archives, 
to create joint physical-digital experiences that showcase their collections in new 
ways [ 134]. 
4.3.5 The Future of Digital Integration in Libraries 
Looking to the future, integrating digital formats in library collections will only 
continue to grow and evolve. As digital technologies become more sophisticated 
and ubiquitous, libraries must be at the forefront of innovation to meet their users’ 
changing needs and expectations [ 
16, 94]. 
One key area of focus will be the development of more personalized and adaptive 
digital experiences. By leveraging data analytics and ML, libraries can create digital 
collections and services that are tailored to the individual needs and preferences of 
each user [ 
92, 120]. This could include personalized recommendations, customized 
search results, and adaptive learning tools that help users discover and engage with 
content more meaningfully. 
Another area of growth will be the use of emerging technologies such as virtual 
reality (VR) and AI to create even more immersive and interactive digital experiences. 
For example, libraries could use VR to create virtual tours of their collections or to 
simulate historical events and environments [
100]. They could also use AI-powered 
chatbots or virtual assistants to provide personalized guidance and support to users 
as they navigate digital collections [ 
84]. 
Ultimately, the success of digital integration in libraries will depend on balancing 
innovation with sustainability and accessibility. Libraries must continue to invest in 
the infrastructure and expertise needed to manage and preserve digital collections 
over the long term while also ensuring that these collections are accessible and 
usable by all members of their communities [ 
76, 90]. This will require ongoing 
collaboration, experimentation, and assessment to identify best practices and adapt 
to the ever-changing digital information landscape. 
Integrating digital formats in library collections represents both an opportunity 
and a challenge for libraries in the 21st century. By embracing digital technologies 
and exploring new ways to blend physical and digital experiences, libraries can 
enhance access, engagement, and preservation of their collections while also meeting 
the evolving needs of their users [ 
94, 100]. However, this integration also requires 
signiﬁcant investments in infrastructure, skills, and innovation and a commitment 
to sustainability and accessibility. As libraries continue to navigate this complex 
landscape, it will be essential to prioritize user needs, collaborate with partners, and 
continuously assess and adapt their approaches to ensure the most signiﬁcant impact 
and value for their communities.

114 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
4.4 Evolution of Online Databases 
The history of online databases reﬂects a continuous commitment to innovation 
within data management. From early developments in the 1960s to today’s advanced 
systems, the progression of these databases has been shaped by the growing needs for 
scalability, ﬂexibility, and enhanced performance [ 
46]. Each phase of this evolution 
has introduced signiﬁcant technological shifts, key breakthroughs, and an ongoing 
effort to leverage data in revolutionary ways. In this section, we will delve into the 
evolution of online databases, tracing their development through various eras, from 
the initial navigational models to the latest advancements in cloud-native and AI-
enhanced systems. Through this exploration, we aim to understand how each phase 
has contributed to the current landscape of data management and anticipate future 
trends that may shape the next generation of database technologies. 
4.4.1 The Navigational Era: Hierarchical and Network 
Models 
The dawn of computerized databases can be traced back to the 1960s when the 
decreasing hardware costs made it feasible for organizations to store and manage 
data electronically. The early database management systems (DBMSs) of this era, 
such as the Integrated Data Store (IDS) developed by Charles Bachman at Gen-
eral Electric and IBM’s Information Management System (IMS), employed naviga-
tional data models [ 
46]. These models, which included the hierarchical and network 
approaches, required users to navigate through the physical structure of the data to 
retrieve information, a process that was inﬂexible and complex [ 
46]. 
While groundbreaking, these navigational databases were inherently limited in 
handling growing data volumes and complexity. This limitation set the stage for 
a revolutionary development that would fundamentally transform the ﬁeld of data 
management. 
4.4.2 The Relational Paradigm: A Transformative Shift 
In 1970, E.F. Codd, a computer scientist at IBM, published his seminal paper “A 
Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks” [ 
30, 46]. This work intro-
duced the relational model, a conceptual framework that proposed structuring data in 
tables consisting of rows and columns, with relationships between tables established 
through shared keys [ 
23]. Codd’s model offered a more ﬂexible and intuitive approach 
to data organization, enabling users to retrieve information using a high-level query 
language based on relational algebra [ 
46].

4.4 Evolution of Online Databases 115
The relational model ushered in a new era of database management, paving the 
way for the development of relational database management systems (RDBMSs) 
such as INGRES and System R, the latter of which introduced the now-ubiquitous 
Structured Query Language (SQL) [
23, 46]. The adoption of the relational model and 
SQL marked a paradigm shift in the industry, providing a standardized and efﬁcient 
means of storing, retrieving, and manipulating data while also offering a level of data 
independence that insulated applications from changes in the underlying physical 
structure [ 
23]. 
4.4.3 The Commercialization of Relational Databases 
The 1980s witnessed the rise of commercial RDBMS products, such as Oracle, 
IBM’s SQL/DS (later DB2), Informix, and Sybase [ 23, 46]. These systems com-
bined the beneﬁts of the relational model with industrial-strength performance, 
reliability, and scalability, enabling organizations to manage increasingly large and 
complex datasets. While object-oriented databases emerged as an alternative during 
this period, relational databases remained the dominant paradigm, bolstered by the 
widespread adoption of SQL as a database standard and the growth of the database 
industry [ 
46]. 
4.4.4 The Web and the Demand for Scalability 
The advent of the World Wide Web in the 1990s ushered in a new era of online 
data and transactions, driving the need for databases that could handle web-scale 
workloads [ 46]. Client-server architectures, with dedicated database servers power-
ing applications, became the norm for web-based systems. This period also saw the 
emergence of open-source databases, such as MySQL and PostgreSQL, which chal-
lenged the dominance of commercial vendors and provided cost-effective solutions 
for web applications [ 
46]. 
As the decade drew to a close, the limitations of relational databases into massive, 
rapidly changing web datasets became increasingly apparent, setting the stage for the 
NoSQL movement [ 
46]. The term “NoSQL” was coined in 1998 to refer to databases 
that used non-SQL query languages and ﬂexible data models, offering an alternative 
to the rigid schemas of traditional relational systems [ 
40]. 
4.4.5 The Rise of NoSQL and Distributed Architectures 
The 2000s witnessed a paradigm shift in database architecture, driven by the need 
for web-scale systems to handle the explosive growth of online data and transac-
tions [ 
25, 37]. The publication of Google’s BigTable paper in 2006 and Amazon’s

116 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
introduction of Dynamo in 2007 laid the foundation for the NoSQL revolution, ush-
ering in a new generation of databases designed from the ground up for scalability, 
ﬂexibility, and distributed architectures [ 25, 37]. NoSQL databases, such as Mon-
goDB, 
Cassandra, Redis, and Neo4j, emerged to address a variety of use cases, 
offering ﬂexible schemas, automatic sharding, and eventual consistency models that 
enabled them to scale across large clusters of commodity servers [ 22, 59]. While pro-
viding 
scalability and ﬂexibility, many of these systems lacked traditional relational 
databases’ strong consistency, transactions, and rich querying capabilities, leading 
to a trade-off between consistency and availability. Nonetheless, NoSQL databases 
were widely adopted for applications where relational databases were not a good ﬁt, 
driving innovation in distributed data management and paving the way for the next 
phase of database evolution. 
4.4.6 The Convergence of SQL and NoSQL 
The 2010s witnessed a convergence of the SQL and NoSQL worlds as vendors sought 
to bridge the gap between the two paradigms. NoSQL databases added transaction 
support, strong consistency, and SQL-like query languages. In contrast, relational 
databases gained features such as JSON support and distributed architectures to 
better compete with NoSQL systems [ 116]. 
This convergence led to the rise of multi-model databases, such as Microsoft’s 
Azure 
Cosmos DB, Google Cloud Spanner, and CockroachDB, which aimed to pro-
vide the scalability and ﬂexibility of NoSQL with the consistency and ease of use of 
relational databases [ 34, 68]. Additionally, the 2010s saw a shift towards cloud-based 
database 
services, with signiﬁcant cloud providers introducing managed offerings 
that simpliﬁed provisioning, scaling, and administration [ 34]. These developments 
pa
ved the way for a new generation of serverless and auto-scaling databases that could 
rapidly adapt to changing workloads, further blurring the lines between traditional 
database architectures. 
4.4.7 The Future of Online Databases: Cloud-Native, 
AI-Augmented, and Beyond 
As we look ahead to the 2020s and beyond, several key trends are shaping the future 
of online databases. Cloud-native databases, built from the ground up for cloud 
deployment, are gaining traction, offering elastic scalability, automatic failover, 
multi-region replication, and consumption-based pricing [ 10 ]. Distributed SQL 
databases 
like CockroachDB, Y ugabyteDB, and PlanetScale are examples of this 
emerging paradigm, designed to take full advantage of cloud infrastructure and 
services [ 68, 85].

4.4 Evolution of Online Databases 117
Moreover, the integration of AI and ML into database systems is enabling a 
new level of intelligence and automation. Intelligent databases can automatically 
optimize queries, detect anomalies, and recommend schema changes. At the same 
time, machine learning techniques are being used to enable predictive analytics and 
augment data management tasks such as data quality and integration [ 
84, 90]. 
The growth of the Internet of Things (IoT), mobile devices, and real-time appli-
cations drives demand for databases that can ingest and process continuous data 
streams with low latency. Event-driven architectures and stream processing engines 
like Apache Kafka and Amazon Kinesis are being integrated with databases to enable 
real-time analytics and decision-making [ 
64, 105]. 
Furthermore, the rise of serverless and edge computing is reshaping the deploy-
ment patterns of databases, with systems like Amazon Aurora and Azure Cos-
mos DB enabling on-demand scaling without the need for infrastructure manage-
ment [ 
38, 114]. On the other hand, Edge databases enable low-latency access to 
data on devices and sensors in the ﬁeld, bringing computation closer to the data 
sources [
109, 124]. 
Emerging technologies such as blockchain and decentralized databases are also 
gaining attention for their ability to provide tamper-proof, auditable records of trans-
actions across multiple parties [ 59, 74]. Enterprise blockchain platforms like Hyper-
ledger Fabric and R3 Corda are being integrated with traditional databases to enable 
secure, multi-party data sharing and collaboration [ 67, 113]. 
4.4.8 The Enduring Pursuit of Innovation 
The evolution of online databases has been remarkable and was marked by a series of 
paradigm shifts and technological breakthroughs that have transformed how we store, 
manage, and analyze data. From the pioneering efforts of the 1960s to the cutting-
edge developments of the present day, this ﬁeld has been driven by a relentless pursuit 
of innovation, fueled by the ever-increasing demands for scalability, ﬂexibility, and 
performance [ 
23, 30, 59]. 
The rise of relational databases in the 1970s and 1980s revolutionized data man-
agement by providing a standardized and efﬁcient means of storing and querying 
structured data [ 
23, 30]. The advent of the World Wide Web and the subsequent 
explosion of web-based applications in the 1990s and 2000s led to the development 
of NoSQL databases and distributed architectures, enabling organizations to handle 
massive amounts of data at unprecedented scales [ 22, 59]. 
As we look to the future, the convergence of cloud computing, AI/machine learn-
ing, and advanced data processing technologies is ushering in a new era of data man-
agement [ 
82, 117]. Cloud databases offer elastic scalability, high availability, and 
pay-as-you-go pricing, making it easier for organizations to handle massive amounts 
of data. AI and machine learning techniques are being integrated into databases to 
enable advanced analytics, predictive modeling, and intelligent automation [ 
3, 98].

118 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
Emerging technologies such as blockchain and edge computing also create new 
opportunities and challenges for data management [ 136, 142]. 
While the future is uncertain, one thing is clear: databases will continue to play 
a critical role in powering the digital services and insights that drive our world. As 
the volume and complexity of data continue to grow, it will be essential for orga-
nizations to adopt modern database technologies and practices to stay competitive 
and drive innovation [ 
61, 82]. This will require technical skills, business acumen, 
and a willingness to embrace change and experimentation. By staying at the fore-
front of database evolution, organizations can unlock new opportunities for growth, 
efﬁciency, and value creation in the digital age. 
4.5 Hybrid Service Models in Modern Libraries 
The advent of the digital age has catalyzed a signiﬁcant transformation in modern 
libraries, necessitating the adoption of hybrid service models that seamlessly inte-
grate traditional physical services with innovative digital offerings. Hybrid libraries 
endeavor to provide patrons with seamless access to information resources across 
multiple formats and delivery methods, catering to the diverse needs of 21st-century 
users [ 
82]. This section delves into the multifaceted nature of hybrid service models 
in contemporary libraries, encompassing digital lending, virtual reference services, 
online academic programs, and the implications for library staff, infrastructure, and 
budgets. 
4.5.1 The Rise of Digital Lending 
Digital lending has become a cornerstone of hybrid library services, empowering 
patrons to access ebooks, audiobooks, and other digital materials remotely. In the 
United States, public libraries witnessed a remarkable 34% surge in digital book 
borrowing between 2019 and 2023 [ 
9]. This burgeoning demand has compelled 
libraries to expand their digital collections and invest in robust lending platforms. 
One innovative approach to digital lending is controlled digital lending (CDL), 
a practice in which libraries circulate temporary digital versions of owned print 
resources on a one-to-one owned-to-loaned ratio. CDL replicates traditional library 
lending in the digital realm by removing the physical copy from circulation while the 
digital version is in use. This practice has gained traction as a means to provide equi-
table access to library materials, particularly for patrons facing barriers to physical 
access [ 
57]. 
However, CDL has also faced legal challenges from publishers who argue that 
the practice infringes on copyright and harms their market. Despite these obstacles, 
many libraries continue to explore CDL to fulﬁll their mission of providing access

4.5 Hybrid Service Models in Modern Libraries 119
to information. CDL can be especially valuable for online students and scholars who 
require access to out-of-print or hard-to-ﬁnd materials [ 47]. 
4.5.2 Virtual Reference Services 
Another critical component of hybrid library models is Virtual Reference Ser-
vices (VRS), which provide professional assistance to patrons through electronic 
means such as email, chat, or video conferencing. VRS extends the reach of tra-
ditional reference desks, allowing librarians to guide patrons in their research and 
information-seeking activities regardless of physical location [ 143]. 
The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of VRS, as libraries sought 
to 
maintain services while physical facilities were closed [ 111]. Many libraries have 
since 
integrated VRS into their regular offerings, recognizing the value of remote 
assistance for patrons unable to visit the library in person. Oregon Tech Library, 
for example, provides 24/7 chat reference through a collaborative service with other 
academic and public libraries in the state [ 99]. 
Effective VRS requires careful planning and implementation. Libraries must 
select 
appropriate communication channels, train staff in virtual reference techniques, 
and develop policies to ensure consistent, high-quality service [144 ]. Additionally, 
libraries 
should regularly evaluate their VRS to identify areas for improvement and 
respond to evolving user needs. 
4.5.3 Online Educational Programs 
Hybrid libraries are also expanding their educational offerings through online pro-
grams and resources. Many academic libraries now provide online tutorials, work-
shops, and course-integrated instruction to support student learning and research 
skills development. These digital offerings complement in-person instruction, 
allowing students to access educational content at their convenience [ 48]. 
Libraries are also collaborating with faculty to create online learning objects and 
modules 
that can be embedded into course management systems. By partnering with 
teaching staff, librarians can ensure that library resources and services are seam-
lessly integrated into the curriculum. This approach fosters a more holistic learning 
experience and reinforces the library’s role as a key partner in education [ 127]. 
In addition to formal instruction, hybrid libraries are curating digital collections 
and 
exhibits that serve as educational resources. Digital archives, special collections, 
and multimedia materials provide rich self-directed learning and exploration oppor-
tunities. By making these unique resources available online, libraries can engage 
learners beyond the conﬁnes of physical spaces.

120 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
4.5.4 Implications for Library Staff, Infrastructure, 
and Budgets 
The shift towards hybrid service models signiﬁcantly affects library staff roles and 
competencies. Librarians in hybrid environments must blend traditional and digital 
skills to navigate physical and virtual spaces easily. This requires ongoing profes-
sional development and training to stay current with emerging technologies and 
service strategies [ 
2]. 
Implementing hybrid service models also necessitates substantial investments in 
technology infrastructure and digital resources. Libraries must have robust systems to 
manage and deliver digital content and reliable networks to support remote access. 
This often involves partnering with vendors and service providers who can offer 
scalable solutions and technical expertise [
138]. 
Budgeting for hybrid services can be complex, as libraries must balance the costs 
of physical materials and spaces with digital resources and platforms. Many libraries 
are shifting their collection development strategies to prioritize electronic formats, 
recognizing the growing demand for remote access. However, this shift can strain 
already limited budgets, particularly as digital content often comes with higher price 
tags and more restrictive licensing terms [ 
77]. 
4.5.5 Embracing Innovation to Serve Patrons 
in the Digital Age 
Hybrid service models represent an exciting frontier for modern libraries, offering 
new ways to engage patrons and fulﬁll the mission of providing access to information. 
By blending physical and digital services, libraries can create a more inclusive and 
responsive environment that meets the diverse needs of 21st-century users [ 
60]. 
However, realizing the full potential of hybrid libraries requires careful planning, 
collaboration, and investment. Libraries must navigate complex legal, technolog-
ical, and organizational challenges as they implement new service models. This 
requires a willingness to experiment, learn from failures, and adapt to changing 
circumstances [
125]. 
Ultimately, hybrid libraries’ success will depend on maintaining a user-centered 
focus while embracing innovation and change. By keeping patrons at the heart of their 
services, libraries can continue to play a vital role in fostering learning, discovery, 
and community engagement in the digital age. 
4.6 Redeﬁning Library Access Methods 
In the rapidly evolving digital landscape, libraries are undergoing a profound transfor-
mation in providing access to resources and services. The traditional model of physi-
cal libraries with print collections is giving way to a more dynamic, technology-driven

4.6 Redeﬁning Library Access Methods 121
approach that emphasizes digital access, mobile services, and cloud-based infrastruc-
ture. This shift is driven by changing user expectations, technological advancements, 
and the need to remain relevant in an increasingly connected world. As libraries nav-
igate this transition, they must reevaluate their access methods to ensure equitable, 
efﬁcient, and user-centered service delivery [ 96]. 
4.6.1 The Rise of Mobile Access 
One of the most signiﬁcant changes in library access is the growing prominence of 
mobile devices. Smartphones and tablets have become ubiquitous, and users increas-
ingly expect to access library resources and services on these devices [ 69]. Library 
users 
are inﬂuenced by technology experiences outside the library, and understanding 
and meeting those expectations is critical. Libraries are responding by developing 
mobile-friendly websites, apps, and services that allow users to search catalogs, 
access e-resources, and interact with the library from anywhere [133 ]. 
Many libraries now offer mobile apps with a streamlined interface for accessing 
library 
services. For example, the EBSCOhost app allows users to search all a library’s 
subscribed EBSCO databases from their mobile device [ 44]. Similarly, the Ex Libris 
Library 
Mobile App offers a branded, personalized experience with integrations to 
library systems like Alma, Primo, and Summon [ 45]. These apps make it easier for 
users 
to discover and access library resources on the go. 
In addition to apps, libraries are optimizing their websites for mobile access. 
Responsi
ve design ensures library websites adapt to different screen sizes and 
devices, providing a seamless user experience. Libraries also implement mobile-
friendly authentication methods, such as the Cisco AnyConnect VPN app, to provide 
secure access to licensed e-resources from off-campus [ 29]. 
The shift towards mobile access is not without challenges. Libraries must consider 
issues 
of accessibility, usability, and digital literacy when designing mobile services. 
They must also ensure that mobile access does not exacerbate existing digital divides 
or create new barriers for users who may not have access to smartphones or reliable 
internet connections. Despite these challenges, the trend toward mobile access is 
clear, and libraries must continue to innovate in this area to meet evolving user 
needs. 
4.6.2 Cloud-Based Infrastructure and Services 
Another major trend in library access is the adoption of cloud-based infrastructure and 
services. Cloud computing offers numerous beneﬁts for libraries, including reduced 
IT costs, increased scalability, improved reliability, and greater ﬂexibility [ 121]. 
By 
moving library systems and services to the cloud, libraries can focus on their

122 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
core mission of providing access to information rather than managing complex IT 
infrastructure. 
One of the most signiﬁcant examples of cloud-based library services is the shift 
to
wards cloud-based library management systems (LMS). Traditional on-premises 
LMS require signiﬁcant maintenance of hardware, software, and staff resources. In 
contrast, cloud-based LMS like OCLC’s WorldShare Management Services (WMS) 
offers a fully integrated, web-based platform that streamlines library workﬂows and 
provides a uniﬁed user experience [ 18]. 
Cloud-based LMS offers numerous advantages over traditional systems. They 
eliminate 
the need for local servers and IT maintenance, reducing costs and freeing 
up staff time [ 88]. They also offer greater scalability, allowing libraries to expand their 
collections 
and services quickly. Additionally, cloud-based systems enable libraries 
to more easily collaborate and share resources with other institutions [ 20]. 
Beyond LMS, libraries adopt other cloud-based services to enhance access and 
user 
experience. For example, many libraries use cloud storage and ﬁle-sharing plat-
forms like Google Drive and Dropbox to facilitate collaboration and resource shar-
ing [ 18]. Cloud-based discovery tools like Ex Libris Primo and EBSCO Discovery 
Service 
provide users with a single search interface for accessing a library’s entire 
collection, including print, electronic, and digital resources [ 8]. 
The move to cloud-based infrastructure and services is not without risks and 
challenges. 
Libraries must carefully evaluate issues of data privacy, security, and 
vendor lock-in when adopting cloud services [ 20]. They must also consider the 
long-term 
sustainability and cost of cloud-based solutions. However, the beneﬁts 
of increased efﬁciency, ﬂexibility, and user experience make cloud computing an 
increasingly attractive option for libraries. 
4.6.3 Accessibility and Universal Design 
As libraries transition to digital access methods, ensuring accessibility for all users is 
a critical concern. Accessibility refers to the design of products, services, and envi-
ronments to be usable by people with a wide range of abilities and disabilities [ 79 ]. In 
the 
library context, this means providing equitable access to resources and services 
regardless of a user’s physical, sensory, or cognitive abilities. 
Universal design is a framework for creating inclusive, accessible spaces and 
services 
that meet the needs of all users. The principles of universal design include 
equitable use, ﬂexibility in use, simple and intuitive design, perceptible information, 
tolerance for error, low physical effort, and size and space for approach and use [ 19]. 
By 
applying these principles to library spaces, technologies, and services, libraries 
can create a more welcoming and inclusive environment for all users [ 106]. 
One key aspect of accessibility in libraries is ensuring that digital resources and 
services 
are usable by people with disabilities. This includes providing alternative for-
mats for materials (e.g., large print, braille, audio), captioning videos, and designing 
websites and apps compatible with assistive technologies like screen readers [ 91].

4.6 Redeﬁning Library Access Methods 123
Libraries must also ensure that physical spaces are accessible, with features like 
ramps, elevators, and adjustable furniture [ 79, 123]. 
Many libraries are embracing universal design as a guiding principle for their ser-
vices and spaces. For example, the University Library at the University of Illinois at 
Urbana-Champaign has implemented several accessibility features to support users 
with disabilities. Adjustable height desks accommodate users of different statures and 
those using mobility devices. The library also provides assistive technology stations 
with software such as screen readers and magniﬁcation tools to access digital content 
for visually impaired users. Additionally, a sensory room offers a calming space for 
users who may become overwhelmed by sensory stimuli, which can be especially 
beneﬁcial for individuals with autism spectrum disorder or sensory processing dis-
orders [
132]. By proactively designing for accessibility, libraries can create a more 
inclusive and equitable environment for all users. 
Accessibility is not just a matter of compliance with legal requirements like the 
Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). It is also a fundamental issue of social justice 
and equal access to information. As libraries continue to evolve their access methods 
in the digital age, prioritizing accessibility and universal design will be essential for 
ensuring that all users can fully participate in the knowledge economy [ 
79]. 
4.6.4 Personalization and User-Centered Design 
Another key trend in library access is the move towards personalization and user-
centered design. In an era of information abundance, users increasingly expect library 
services and interfaces to be tailored to their needs and preferences [ 52]. Personal-
ization can take many forms, from customized search results and recommendations 
to targeted content and alerts based on a user’s interests and behavior. 
One example of personalization in libraries is the use of adaptive learning tech-
nologies. These systems use data analytics and machine learning to provide person-
alized learning experiences based on a user’s strengths, weaknesses, and learning 
style [
141]. For instance, the University of Michigan Library has implemented an 
adaptive learning platform called ECoach. It provides personalized study tips and 
resources for students based on their course performance and engagement [ 
15]. 
Another area is using recommendation systems to help users discover rele-
vant resources. Many library discovery tools now incorporate recommendation fea-
tures that suggest related materials based on a user’s search history and borrowing 
patterns [ 
24]. 
Personalization is closely related to the concept of user-centered design, which 
puts the needs and preferences of users at the center of the design process. User-
centered design involves techniques like user research, persona development, and 
usability testing to ensure that library services and interfaces are intuitive, efﬁcient, 
and satisfying to use [ 78]. By designing with users in mind, libraries can create more 
engaging and compelling digital experiences.

124 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
One example of user-centered design in libraries is the development of vir-
tual browsing interfaces that mimic the serendipitous discovery of physical library 
shelves. The Harvard Library Innovation Lab’s StackLife project uses virtual reality 
technology to allow users to browse a 3D representation of the library’s print col-
lection, complete with book covers and spines [ 
75]. Virtual reality and augmented 
reality technologies are increasingly used in libraries to enhance the user experience 
and provide immersive ways to explore library collections [ 
83]. This immersive, 
visual browsing type can help users ﬁnd unexpected connections and resources that 
traditional search interfaces may miss. 
As libraries continue to evolve their digital access methods, personalization and 
user-centered design will be key strategies for meeting the diverse needs and expec-
tations of users [
110]. By leveraging data, technology, and user insights, libraries 
can create more engaging, efﬁcient, and discoverable digital experiences that keep 
users returning. 
4.6.5 Collaboration and Resource Sharing 
In addition to enhancing local access, libraries are also increasingly collaborating and 
sharing resources on a regional, national, and global scale. Resource sharing allows 
libraries to expand their collections and services beyond what they could provide 
individually while reducing costs and duplication of effort. Collaborative networks 
and consortia enable libraries to share expertise, infrastructure, and best practices, 
leading to more efﬁcient and effective service delivery [ 
21]. 
One of the most well-established forms of library collaboration is interlibrary loan 
(ILL), which allows users to request materials from other libraries when unavail-
able locally. ILL has traditionally been a manual, paper-based process, but many 
libraries now use automated, cloud-based ILL systems to streamline requests and 
delivery [ 
89]. For example, the ILLiad system from OCLC allows libraries to manage 
the entire ILL process online, from request to delivery [ 95]. 
Beyond ILL, libraries also participate in shared print initiatives that allow them to 
manage and preserve print collections collaboratively. Shared print programs involve 
libraries agreeing to retain and share certain materials while allowing other partici-
pating libraries to withdraw duplicates and free up space [ 1]. For example, the Eastern 
Academic Scholars’ Trust (EAST) is a shared print initiative involving over 75 aca-
demic libraries in the eastern United States [ 43]. By collaborating on print retention, 
libraries can ensure long-term access to materials while reducing storage costs and 
space pressures. 
Another area of collaboration is the development of shared digital repositories and 
collections. Many libraries are partnering to create digital libraries that aggregate and 
preserve unique or rare materials from multiple institutions [
115]. For example, the 
HathiTrust Digital Library is a partnership of over 200 academic and research libraries

4.7 Digital Transformation in Response to Global Challenges 125
that have contributed millions of digitized books and documents to a shared reposi-
tory [ 58]. By pooling resources and expertise, libraries can create more prosperous 
and 
more comprehensive digital collections than they could on their own [ 129]. 
Collaborative networks and consortia allow libraries to share expertise and best 
practices 
in digital access and services. For example, the Digital Library Federation 
(DLF) is a community of practitioners who advance research, learning, and the public 
good through digital library technologies [ 39]. DLF provides a forum for libraries 
to 
share knowledge, develop standards and best practices, and collaborate on digital 
access, preservation, and user experience projects. 
As digital access becomes increasingly central to library services, collaboration, 
and 
resource sharing will be essential strategies for expanding collections, reducing 
costs, and enhancing user experience [ 21]. By working together across institutional 
boundaries, 
libraries can create a more seamless and sustainable digital information 
ecosystem that beneﬁts users worldwide [ 7]. 
4.7 Digital Transformation in Response to Global 
Challenges 
The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the digital transformation of libraries, 
compelling them to adapt rapidly to a new reality where physical spaces are limited 
and digital services are essential. This transformation has not only been a response 
to the immediate challenges posed by the pandemic but also a catalyst for long-term 
changes in how libraries serve their communities. The pandemic has highlighted the 
critical role of libraries in supporting education, research, and public health while 
also exposing the digital divide that exists in many communities. 
This section explores the various aspects of digital transformations in libraries 
in 
response to global challenges, focusing on the COVID-19 pandemic. It examines 
how libraries have adapted their services, collections, and spaces to meet the needs 
of their users in a socially distanced world and how these adaptations may shape the 
future of libraries in the post-pandemic era. 
4.7.1 Supporting Remote Learning and Research 
One of the most signiﬁcant challenges libraries face during the pandemic has been the 
need to support remote learning and research. With schools and universities closed 
or operating online, students and faculty have relied heavily on digital resources to 
continue their studies and work. Libraries have responded by expanding their digital 
collections, increasing access to ebooks, e-journals, and databases, and providing 
remote support services [ 42].

126 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
For example, the Public Health Digital Library (PHDL) has been a vital resource 
for public health departments during the pandemic, providing access to over 
290 journals, 80+ ebooks, and multiple databases. The PHDL has enabled pub-
lic health professionals to access the latest research and evidence-based practices 
related to COVID-19, helping them make informed decisions and develop effective 
interventions [ 
93]. 
Academic libraries have also played a crucial role in supporting distance education 
during the pandemic. Information technology and online libraries are increasingly 
important in creating creative spaces for distance learning. Libraries have collab-
orated with faculty to integrate digital resources into online courses, provided vir-
tual reference services, and created online tutorials and workshops to help students 
develop research skills [ 
41]. 
However, the rapid shift to remote learning has also highlighted the digital divide 
in many communities. Not all students have access to reliable internet or devices 
at home, making participating fully in online learning challenging. Libraries have 
sought to bridge this divide by providing Wi-Fi hotspots, laptops, and other equipment 
for checkout, as well as offering socially distanced computer access in their physical 
spaces [ 
42]. 
4.7.2 Curating and Disseminating Reliable Information 
Another critical role libraries have played during the pandemic is curating and dis-
seminating reliable information about COVID-19. With the proliferation of misin-
formation and conspiracy theories online, libraries have served as trusted sources of 
accurate, up-to-date information for their communities. Many libraries have created 
dedicated COVID-19 resource guides on their websites, compiling links to govern-
ment agencies, health organizations, and other authoritative sources. They have also 
used social media platforms to share reliable information and combat the spread of 
misinformation. Librarians have also been involved in more proactive efforts to pro-
mote public health information. For example, the Network of the National Library 
of Medicine (NNLM) has partnered with public libraries to provide training and 
resources on health literacy, helping librarians better understand and communicate 
complex health information to their patrons [ 
93]. 
4.7.3 Reimagining Physical Spaces 
While much of the focus during the pandemic has been on digital services, libraries 
have also had to reimagine their physical spaces to ensure the safety of their staff 
and patrons. This has involved implementing social distancing measures, increasing 
cleaning and sanitation protocols, and reconﬁguring spaces for better ventilation 
and trafﬁc ﬂow. Some libraries have also experimented with new service models,

4.7 Digital Transformation in Response to Global Challenges 127
such as curbside pickup and outdoor programming, to maintain a physical presence 
in their communities while minimizing the risk of COVID-19 transmission. These 
adaptations have required signiﬁcant creativity and ﬂexibility from library staff and 
close collaboration with local health authorities and community partners [ 140]. 
4.7.4 Looking to the Future 
As libraries continue to navigate the challenges of the pandemic, they are also looking 
to the future and considering how the digital transformation of the past year may 
shape their services and spaces in the long term. Many changes implemented out of 
necessity, such as expanded digital collections and virtual programming, are likely 
to become permanent ﬁxtures of library services. However, libraries will also need 
to grapple with the ongoing challenges of the digital divide and the evolving needs of 
their communities in a post-pandemic world. This may involve continued investment 
in technology infrastructure and digital literacy programs, as well as a renewed 
focus on equity and inclusion in library services. Libraries may also need to rethink 
their physical spaces to accommodate a hybrid in-person and digital services model. 
This could involve creating more ﬂexible, multi-use spaces that adapt to changing 
needs and incorporating more technology and digital displays to enhance the user 
experience [ 128]. 
4.7.5 Libraries’ Pandemic-Driven Digital Transformation 
The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the digital transformation of libraries, 
forcing them to adapt quickly to a new reality where physical spaces are limited 
and digital services are essential. Libraries have risen to the challenge of expanding 
their digital collections, providing remote support for learning and research, curating 
reliable information, and reimagining their physical spaces. While the pandemic has 
been a catalyst for change, it has also exposed the ongoing challenges of the digital 
divide and the need for continued investment in technology infrastructure and digital 
literacy programs. As libraries look to the future, they will need to balance the beneﬁts 
of digital transformation with the importance of maintaining equitable access and 
inclusive services for all members of their communities. 
Ultimately, the role of libraries in supporting education, research, and pub-
lic 
knowledge has never been more critical. By embracing digital transformation 
and adapting to the challenges of the pandemic, libraries have demonstrated their 
resilience and enduring value to society. As we move forward into an uncertain 
future, libraries will continue to evolve and innovate to meet the changing needs of 
their communities.

128 4 Digital Transformation: Reshaping Access and Engagement
4.8 Chapter Summary 
Chapter 4 thoroughly examines the seismic shift that libraries are undergoing due 
to advancements in digital technology and changing user expectations. The chapter 
identiﬁes critical drivers of this transformation, such as the digital-ﬁrst expectations of 
users, competition from readily accessible online sources, and operational challenges 
spurred by ﬁnancial constraints and the recent COVID-19 pandemic. It explores 
the myriad opportunities digital transformation presents for libraries, including the 
expansion of digital collections, the adoption of innovative technologies like AI 
and mobile applications, and the reimagining of library spaces to accommodate 
digital learning and creation. These advancements not only enable libraries to offer 
personalized and accessible services but also position them as essential players in 
bridging the digital divide through technology access and digital literacy programs. 
However, the chapter does not overlook these digital shifts’ signiﬁcant challenges. 
It delves into issues such as copyright complexities, data privacy concerns, the sus-
tainability of digital services, and the pressing need to address the digital divide 
comprehensively. The analysis underscores the importance of strategic planning and 
continuous innovation for libraries to navigate these challenges successfully. It advo-
cates for a balanced approach that leverages technology to enhance library services 
while ensuring equitable access and maintaining the core mission of libraries as 
community hubs of knowledge and learning. 
In summary, Chap. 4 offers a nuanced analysis of the digital transformation 
in libraries, balancing the excitement around digital opportunities with a sober-
ing acknowledgment of the challenges ahead. It calls for a strategic and adaptable 
approach, emphasizing the need for libraries to innovate while remaining steadfast in 
their commitment to accessibility and user-centered services. This chapter serves as 
both a roadmap and a cautionary tale for libraries navigating the complex terrain of 
the digital age, highlighting the critical role of libraries in ensuring that the beneﬁts 
of digital transformation are accessible to all members of society.
